title: Other Classifications
short: State laws discriminating against lawfully present noncitizens usually get strict scrutiny (Graham v. Richardson, 1971); classifications by legitimacy get intermediate scrutiny; age (Massachusetts Board of Retirement v. Murgia, 1976), wealth (San Antonio v. Rodriguez, 1973) and disability (Cleburne) get rational basis.
trouble: Students think every disadvantaged group gets heightened scrutiny. The Court has declined to add new suspect classes since the 1970s; age, wealth and disability get rational basis.

blocks.html: Note: This is an educational course, not legal advice.

After race and sex, which other classifications get closer review? The answers come from the factors in the framework (history of discrimination, an unchangeable trait, political powerlessness) and from rational basis cases.

head: Classification
Tier
Leading case and notes
rows: State laws about lawfully present noncitizens (alienage)
Graham v. Richardson (1971): exception: states may limit "political functions" such as police officers and public school teachers to citizens; federal immigration rules get deference
the Court's legitimacy cases: children should not be penalized for their parents' status
Massachusetts Board of Retirement v. Murgia (1976): mandatory retirement for state police at 50 upheld
San Antonio Independent School District v. Rodriguez (1973): school funding through local property taxes upheld
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center (1985): though the denial in Cleburne failed even that test
Children not lawfully present, denied schooling
Plyler v. Doe (1982): struck down: the law did not further a substantial state goal

blocks.html: The Court has been reluctant to add new suspect classes. In Murgia it said older people have not faced a history of purposeful unequal treatment like that based on race, and everyone who lives long enough becomes old. In Rodriguez it said the poor are not a definite class and wealth-based lines are common in economic life. In Cleburne it said people with intellectual disabilities have real differences that legislatures address with many laws, often protective ones, and closer review could discourage that legislation. Plyler v. Doe is hard to classify: the majority, noting that children do not choose their status and that denying education imposes a lifetime hardship, asked whether the law furthered a "substantial" state goal. Four justices dissented, saying it was a policy question for the legislature. Courts and scholars still debate what tier Plyler applied.

blocks.name: cv-scrutiny
blocks.cap: State alienage classifications: usually strict scrutiny.

blocks.html: Beyond race and sex: state alienage laws usually get strict scrutiny (with a political-function exception); legitimacy gets intermediate; age, wealth and disability get rational basis. The Court has declined to add new suspect classes since the 1970s.

blocks.title: Political function
blocks.q: A state requires its police officers to be U.S. citizens. Strict scrutiny?
steps: State alienage classifications usually get strict scrutiny (Graham).
But the Court has allowed states to limit jobs that carry out basic governmental functions, like police officers, to citizens, reviewed only for rationality.
blocks.a: No; the political-function exception applies, and the rule is upheld.

blocks.title: Age
blocks.q: A state requires judges to retire at 70. A 70-year-old judge sues under equal protection. Tier and likely result?
steps: Age is not a suspect class (Murgia).
Rational basis: the state might rationally worry about declining abilities in some people, even if not in this judge.
The Court upheld Missouri's judicial retirement age in Gregory v. Ashcroft (1991), on other grounds as well.

blocks.html: Thinking every disadvantaged group gets heightened scrutiny. The Court has declined to add new suspect classes since the 1970s: age, wealth and disability get rational basis. Heightened review comes from the established list (race, national origin, state alienage, sex, legitimacy) or from a burden on a fundamental right.
